newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says conditions not ripe for NATO return.
newsitem.headline: France says conditions not ripe for NATO return.

text.p: France said on Wednesday the conditions were not yet ripe for it to return to full membership of NATO's military wing, which it quit in 1966 in protest at U.S. domination.
It also insisted that five new ex-communist countries were qualified to join the Atlantic Alliance, not just the three accepted by the United States.

In a statement issued after conservative President Jacques Chirac discussed the issue with Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, the Foreign Ministry said France wanted "to continue discussions with its allies to seek a better balance of responsibilities between Europeans and Americans."

The statement set the scene for a possibly tense NATO summit in Madrid next week, at which Chirac could clash with U.S. President Bill Clinton both on transatlantic power-sharing and on the shape of the alliance's eastward enlargement.

It made clear that Chirac, who initiated a rapprochement with NATO in 1995, shared the new left-wing French government's view that Washington had not yielded sufficient power to the European allies to justify a return.
Paris has demanded in vain that Washington hand over NATO's key southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to a European officer.

The Clinton administration bluntly refused and effectively declared negotiations to be ended on June 12 after France elected a Socialist-led government critical of a full reintegration into the allied command structure.

"In the current state of negotiations, while noting that progress has been achieved, notably in affirming a European defence identity, France considers that the conditions it posed for re-examining its relations with NATO's military structures are not met," the statement said.

"On enlargement, France reaffirms that five countries now meet the conditions for joining the Alliance," the ministry said, alluding to Romania and Slovenia, as well as the three Washington accepts: the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland.

Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi telephoned Chirac on Wednesday to discuss preparations for the summit, at which both countries will argue for a wider enlargement to underscore NATO's commitment to security in the Black Sea and the Balkans.
Jospin will not attend the July 8-9 summit, which the statement called "an important moment for the alliance, both for its renovation and to start the process of enlargement".
Chirac's office reacted with irritation last Friday when the Socialist-run Foreign Ministry made known its assessment without waiting for the president's formal decision.

Aides to the president noted that the consensus text issued "in the name of the French authorities" after Chirac chaired an inner cabinet meeting on Wednesday included a willingness to continue the negotiations.

The United States has agreed in principle that a European deputy to the American Supreme Allied Commander in Europe would take charge of operations in which Washington chose not to participate, overseeing a European chain of command within the NATO structure.
But NATO sources said the Madrid summit was unlikely to approve a limited reform of the alliance's command structure because of the persistant Franco-American differences.
Other allies such as Britain and the Netherlands would not be willing to give up jobs in a partial reshuffle that may have to be reopened if a deal was reached with France, they said.
